The daily cleaning of restrooms is documented on a \u201cRestroom Cleaning Log\u201d located on the back of the door, visible when exiting each restroom, thus allowing the public to see when the restroom was last cleaned. All public restrooms also have signage posted on the wall stating the phone number to contact if the restroom does not meet the standards of the user. An EMS Technician (EMS Tech) has been assigned to regularly inspect high-traffic restrooms in public areas during each business day to continuously maintain cleanliness. Twenty-four standard operating procedures (SOP), to include dusting, exam room and restroom cleaning/disinfection, have been implemented to guide and maintain the routine cleaning/disinfection of the facility by EMS staff. EMS staff training on the updated procedures and expectations was completed on June 2, 2026. Oversight of cleanliness throughout the facility is conducted on a daily basis by the Chief of EMS. All employees throughout the healthcare system were informed of their role in maintaining a clean, safe, and healthy environment for our Veteran patients during an all-employee town hall held on June 2, 2026. Facility\u2019s Actions Responsive to OIG Inspection Additionally, the OIG found the primary care and women\u2019s health clinics had multiple clean pieces of equipment and supplies stored in the soiled utility room. VHA Directive 1131, Management of Infectious Diseases and Infection Prevention and Control Programs requires staff to store clean and soiled items separately to prevent infections.17 The nurse manager was unable to explain why staff stored the items together. The Associate Director was unaware of the issue and said the OIG\u2019s findings highlighted new areas to focus on during routine inspections. An executive leader submitted information in December 2025 that confirmed separate rooms were designated to store soiled and clean items. Staff also reported they are inspecting these areas monthly to verify appropriate storage. Therefore, the OIG did not make a recommendation. The primary care clinic had expired respiratory masks in a clean storage room. The nurse manager reported that nursing staff posted a note with instructions not to use the masks because the manufacturer\u2019s expiration date had passed. However, the supply chain chief said guidance to clinic staff is to discard the expired supplies or return them. The comprehensive environment of care committee coordinator said members were unaware of the expired items because they have not inspected the storage room in six months. Staff said this was due to the room being locked during environment of care rounds. A committee member noted that a supervisor for the area can unlock the door if they are participating in the inspection rounds. The OIG did not make a recommendation because the supervisory safety manager reported in December 2025 that members of the environment of care team now have access to all spaces, including restricted areas. Staff discussed an ongoing issue with an emergency alert system at an outpatient clinic. The system enables staff, patients, and visitors to send an alert when they require help. Staff expressed concern that after someone pulls the alarm, the system cannot be reactivated until it is reset. The chief of police explained that because the reset button is in the police station, a police officer must be present to grant access to staff. The deputy chief of engineering submitted information in December 2025 that verified staff had relocated the emergency alert system from the locked police station to a corridor accessible to nursing staff, and therefore, the OIG did not make a recommendation. Finally, there was a damaged concrete floor in a women\u2019s restroom. The damage created an uneven surface, which increases fall risks, especially for those who use assistive walking devices. ### 3. Key Areas to Focus for the Upcoming Inspection  

1. **Environment of Care (EOC) – Cleanliness & Safety**  
   - Verify daily restroom cleaning logs are posted and up‑to‑date.  
   - Confirm all 24 SOPs are accessible, staff have completed the 6 Jun 2026 training, and the Chief of EMS conducts daily oversight.  
   - Review the weekly EOC rounds checklist and ensure the Associate Director’s attendance is documented.  
   - Check that clean/soiled item storage segregation (VHA Directive 1131) is maintained and that expired supplies (e.g., respiratory masks) are removed promptly.

2. **Primary‑Care – Toxic‑Exposure Screening**  
   - Ensure the SOP for secondary TES is finalized, communicated, and that providers are following it.  
   - Validate monthly CEC reports showing zero unresolved secondary TES > 30 days.  
   - Document any gaps and corrective actions before the 31 Dec 2026 target.

3. **Information Technology – Data‑Center Controls**  
   - Confirm a functional video‑surveillance system is installed, recorded, and monitored per OIT standards.  
   - Verify water‑detection sensors are installed and tested; produce maintenance logs.  

4. **Test‑Result Communication** *(high‑frequency peer issue)*  
   - Even though not cited at El Paso, review VHA Directive 1088 compliance: have service‑level workflows been drafted? Is there staff education on abnormal result follow‑up within 7 days?  
   - Prepare documentation of any existing processes to show proactive compliance.

5. **Leadership & Governance**  
   - Document VISN‑level support and any actions taken to ensure stable leadership.  
   - Provide evidence of performance‑improvement plans for recurring themes (e.g., EOC trends, TES metrics).

### 5. How to Use This Information  

- **During the OIG inspection:** Provide the specific OIG citation for each item you discuss (e.g., “Report 25‑00193‑155, https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system”).  
- **For internal tracking:** Keep the target dates and status fields from the “own_history” section as your baseline; update them as you close recommendations.  
- **When responding to OIG questions:** Quote the exact language from the findings (e.g., “Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment.”) and show how your corrective actions satisfy that language.

---

**Bottom line:** Focus on the four open recommendations, especially the Environment of Care and Primary‑Care actions that have clear target dates, and be prepared to demonstrate compliance with high‑frequency peer themes such as test‑result communication and clean‑environment standards.
